strengths: Strong empirical results: Video-o3-7B outperforms prior open-source single-turn, decoupled, and native tool-use models across seven benchmarks (e.g., 72.1 on MLVU, 47.6 on LVBench, 46.5 on Video-Holmes, 60.7 mIoU on Charades-STA), establishing a clear state-of-the-art at matched model scale.

Comprehensive ablation suite: the paper dissects TDAM components (Table 3), VTGR sub-components (Table 4), mask ratios (Table 9), training-stage contributions (Table 10), turn limits (Table 5), and training dynamics (Figures 8-9), which substantiates each design choice rather than relying only on end-to-end comparisons.

End-to-end verifiability framing is well executed: the four-stage data synthesis pipeline (clue localization, validity verification, trajectory generation, logical consistency check) with a four-quadrant task taxonomy and full dataset statistics (Table 6) is a concrete, reusable contribution.

Unusually complete reproducibility material: full hyperparameter tables (Tables 7-8), prompt templates (Figure 10), tool-quota formulation (Appendix A), and the over-turn masked GRPO objective (Appendix B) are provided.

Honest treatment of weaknesses: the paper includes a dedicated failure-case analysis (Appendix H), 'fake thinking' case studies (Appendix I), and a limitations section on context depth and tool scalability, which is commendable.

Efficiency analysis (Table 11) demonstrates that the shared-context design yields a real 33-46% inference speedup over decoupled iterative baselines alongside higher accuracy, supporting the core paradigm claim.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the method largely composes existing techniques (Qwen2.5-VL backbone, DAPO/GRPO, Mini-o3's over-turn masking) with two modest additions - an attention-masking heuristic for SFT and a hand-tuned reward multiplier. Neither is analyzed at depth (e.g., no theoretical or mechanistic understanding of why masking only 10% of data works).

TDAM ablation evidence is thin and internally inconsistent: gains over the no-mask baseline are 0.8-3.9 points, but in Table 3 the partial variants ('w/o ans. mask', 'w/o gr. mask') beat the full method on LongVideoBench (57.0/57.1 vs 56.6) and VideoMMMU, suggesting the full-mask superiority may be within noise; no variance estimates or significance tests are reported anywhere.

Potential benchmark contamination is not addressed: training data is drawn from LLaVA-Video, CGBench, self-collected YouTube, and synthetic data generated with Gemini 2.5 Pro, yet the paper does not discuss overlap checking with evaluation benchmarks (MLVU, LongVideoBench, VideoMME), which is a material concern for SOTA claims.

Comparisons with baselines may not be fully controlled: frame budgets, token budgets, and decoding settings of competing methods are not reported uniformly, and the headline improvements on some benchmarks (e.g., 66.5 vs 65.2 on VideoMME) are modest relative to the added system complexity.

The 'verifiable' reward depends on synthetic ground-truth clue intervals and an annotated reference turn count k_ref, both produced by the same VLM/LLM pipeline; label noise in these signals is not quantified, and possible reward-hacking behaviors (e.g., gaming the IoU-based score without genuinely better seeking) are not examined.
Only multiple-choice accuracy is reported; no open-ended QA metrics or human evaluation, so reasoning quality beyond MC accuracy is unverified.

Some references appear implausible or unfinished (future-dated arXiv IDs such as 2511/2512, 'GPT-5.2', 'Gemini 3 Pro'), and no explicit code/data release statement is made, which weakens reproducibility despite detailed hyperparameters.

strengths: The system-level contribution is well-executed: native multi-turn interleaved tool invocation (VideoCrop with model-controlled temporal segments and visual token quotas) is a coherent alternative to decoupled iterative reasoning pipelines, and the KV-cache-based shared context yields a concrete efficiency gain (10.2s vs 15.2-18.9s inference on MLVU, Table 11).

The evaluation is broad (seven video QA benchmarks plus temporal grounding) and the paper outperforms same-size (7B) open-source competitors on most of them, e.g., 72.1% on MLVU and 46.5% on Video-Holmes.

Ablations are unusually thorough for this line of work: TDAM components (Table 3), VTGR components (Table 4), mask ratio (Table 9), max-turn budget (Table 5), training-stage decomposition (Table 10), and training dynamics curves (Figs. 8-9), with implementation details and prompts supplied in the appendix.

The paper is transparent about weaknesses: the 'fake thinking' phenomenon (Appendix I) motivating TDAM, failure cases from turn-limit exhaustion (Fig. 14), and an honest limitations section discussing context-depth and tool-scalability constraints.

The Seeker-173K data pipeline (clue localization, validity verification, trajectory generation, logical consistency check) is described in enough detail, with a four-quadrant task taxonomy, that the training methodology could in principle be rebuilt.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is limited. Native multi-turn tool invocation for video MLLMs is already explored by Mini-o3, Video-Zoomer, Conan, LongVT, and VideoChat-R1.5; the proposed mechanisms (an attention mask separating SFT phases, an IoU-style grounding bonus, and a turn-count decay penalty in GRPO) are straightforward engineering refinements rather than new insights. The framing overstates the distinction from prior 'decoupled' work.

Potential train/test contamination is not addressed. Table 6 shows the training data is built from CG-Bench and LongVideoDB, and the model is evaluated on LVBench, LongVideoBench, VideoMME, etc., largely drawn from LLaVA-Video-sourced videos; the possibility of benchmark overlap with training videos or questions is neither discussed nor checked, which undercuts the headline SOTA claims.

Statistical rigor is weak. All results use deterministic greedy decoding in a single run with no variance, error bars, or significance tests, yet several pivotal ablation deltas are small (e.g., Table 3: full TDAM 44.2 vs. 44.1 for either partial mask on LVBench; Table 4 gains of +1.4 to +2.8). It is unclear which component gains are reliable.

Fairness of comparisons is unclear: frame sampling rate, visual token budget, and prompt format for baselines are not standardized or reported, and gains may partly reflect a much larger visual token quota (16k overview tokens, up to 768 frames) rather than the proposed training innovations.

No commitment to releasing code, models, or the Seeker-173K dataset; moreover, 14.8k self-collected YouTube instances are used without any discussion of copyright, licensing, or redistribution rights, which is an ethics/reproducibility gap.

The data pipeline depends on Gemini 2.5 Pro for clue localization and CoT generation, which introduces cost, licensing ambiguity around distillation from a closed model, and an unquantified dependence on teacher quality that is never ablated.

The 'state-of-the-art' claim is scoped only to 7B open-source models; comparisons against larger open models or the closed-source models used in the pipeline (e.g., Gemini 2.5 Pro) are absent, so the practical significance of the numbers is hard to gauge.

Several design choices are justified only empirically and ad hoc (e.g., masking applied to 10% of tool-use data; the specific reward constants b0=0.5, wg=0.5, Cfree=0.5, lambda=0.05), and sensitivity analyses for the reward hyperparameters are not provided.

strengths: Comprehensive system contribution: the paper combines a training recipe (SFT cold start + RL), a masking mechanism (TDAM), a shaped reward (VTGR), and a large synthesized trajectory dataset (Seeker-173K), and demonstrates that native multi-turn tool invocation is trainable end-to-end rather than via hand-crafted heuristics.

Broad and mostly convincing empirical evaluation across seven video QA benchmarks plus temporal grounding (Charades-STA), with consistent (if sometimes modest) improvements over strong recent baselines such as LOVE-R1, Conan, and Video-Zoomer.

Unusually thorough ablation studies for this area: component-wise ablations of TDAM and VTGR, mask-ratio sweeps, max-turn analysis, training-stage analysis, and an inference-efficiency comparison (Table 11) that plausibly attributes the speedup to KV-cache reuse in shared-context inference.

Honest and useful limitations discussion (Appendix H/J), including a failure case analysis and case studies of the 'fake thinking' phenomenon, which is a genuinely interesting observation about faithfulness in tool-augmented reasoning.
Reasonable reproducibility support: full hyperparameter tables, prompt templates, data source breakdown, and framework choices (LLaMA-Factory, verl, vLLM) are documented.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: TDAM is a straightforward attention-masking heuristic and VTGR is conventional reward shaping (IoU-style localization bonus + turn-count penalty) applied on top of existing infrastructure (Mini-o3's over-turn masking, DAPO/GRPO). The contribution is largely engineering integration and data curation rather than a new methodological insight.

Potential train/test contamination is not addressed: the training corpus is heavily sourced from LLaVA-Video, CGBench, LongVideoDB, etc., while evaluation uses benchmarks (VideoMME, MLVU, LongVideoBench, CG-Bench-derived tasks) whose source videos substantially overlap with such corpora. No decontamination analysis or statement is provided, which is a significant threat to the claimed SOTA results.

Headline claims of 'substantial' outperformance are overstated: gains over the best prior native-tool baselines are often ~1 point (VideoMME 66.5 vs 65.2; MMVU 67.2 vs 66.9), and the SFT+RL vs RL-only deltas are ~0.4 points. No variance, seeds, or significance testing is reported.

Ablation evidence for the two core proposed components is noisy and internally inconsistent: in Table 3, 'w/o gr. mask' beats the full model on LongVideoBench (57.1 vs 56.6) and Video-Holmes (40.8 vs 41.3); in Table 4, 'w/o Turn Decay Factor' is close to or better on LongVideoBench; in Table 9 the mask-ratio results are non-monotonic. These patterns suggest differences within run-to-run noise, weakening the causal claims for TDAM and the decay factor.

Comparative fairness concerns: baseline numbers are cited from prior reports rather than re-run under a unified protocol, and the Charades-STA comparison in Table 2 mixes models designed for different regimes (LongVT performs far below even Qwen2.5-VL there, making the comparison somewhat uninformative).
Parts of the self-collected data (14.8k YouTube instances) and the dataset release status are unspecified, which limits full reproducibility of the RL results.

The claimed mechanism behind TDAM ('attention dispersion') is supported only indirectly by end-task metrics; no attention statistics or behavioral analysis directly verifies the hypothesized cause, and the 10% masking ratio appears tuned post hoc.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across eight video QA benchmarks plus temporal grounding (Charades-STA), with results compared against single-turn, decoupled iterative, and native multi-turn baselines at matched model scale (7B), including reproduced baselines under a unified evaluation protocol.

Thorough ablation studies: TDAM masking components and mask ratios (Tables 3, 11), VTGR sub-components (Table 4, Figs. 8-9), max-turn limits (Table 5), turn distributions (Table 13), training stages (Table 14), and data-scalability with free-format data (Table 15) — this level of analysis substantially exceeds typical practice.

The 'fake thinking' phenomenon (Appendix I) motivating Task-Decoupled Attention Masking is an interesting, well-documented observation, and the accompanying Charades-STA ablation (Table 12) gives direct evidence that the Hybrid Clue Score improves localization rather than just tool-call frequency.

Efficiency analysis (Table 6) credibly shows the shared-context multi-turn paradigm is faster and cheaper in tokens than decoupled iterative methods, supporting the paper's central design claim; generalization to a 4B base model (Table 7) adds evidence the recipe transfers.

Honest and detailed treatment of limitations (Appendix J), failure cases (Appendix H), prompts, and full hyperparameter tables, plus a substantive impact statement addressing surveillance/privacy risks.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the pipeline is assembled largely from existing components — DAPO (Yu et al., 2025b), over-turn masking from Mini-o3 (Lai et al., 2025), and the multi-turn crop-and-inspect paradigm from Conan, Video-Zoomer, LongVT, and VideoChat-R1.5. The genuinely new pieces (TDAM applied to only 10% of SFT data, the VTGR multiplier) are heuristic engineering with several hand-tuned hyperparameters (b0, wg, Cfree, λ) whose sensitivity is only partially explored.

Reward and bonus design is not analytically justified: ablation deltas are small on some benchmarks (e.g., Table 3: w/o grounding mask 44.1 vs. 44.2 on LVBench; Table 4: w/o Turn Decay Factor is 46.7 vs. 47.5 on LVBench and even higher than the full system on some cells), and no variance/significance reporting is provided, making some component-level claims hard to distinguish from noise.

Potential train/test contamination is not addressed: a large fraction of training data is sourced from LLaVA-Video (Table 8), whose corpus is known to overlap with evaluated benchmarks (e.g., VideoMME, LongVideoBench); the paper reports no decontamination procedure, which weakens headline SOTA claims.

Heavy dependence on a closed frontier model (Gemini) for data synthesis, and unclear commitment to releasing Seeker-173K, code, or the 14.8k self-collected YouTube instances; reproducibility of the RL reward pipeline (which needs reference clue intervals and per-sample turn annotations) is therefore uncertain.

Presentation inconsistencies undermine confidence: duplicated </grounding> tags in examples and prompts, 'Gemini 2.5 Pro' vs. 'Gemini 3 pro' mismatch, quota figures inconsistent across Figures 1/3, and several typos; the abstract reports 72.1%/46.5% while the narrative attributes the best numbers variously to RL-only vs. SFT+RL variants without fully clarifying which configuration is 'the' model.

strengths: The evaluation is broad: eight video QA benchmarks, temporal grounding (Charades-STA), an efficiency comparison (Table 6), generalization to a smaller base model (Table 7), and a large set of ablations (Tables 3-5, 11-15) with training curves (Figures 8-9).
The paper is generally well organized and clearly written, with a comprehensible description of the training pipeline, reward design, and hyperparameters (Tables 9-10, prompt templates in Figure 10).

The data synthesis pipeline and Seeker-173K dataset are described in enough detail (Section 4, Appendix C, Figures 6-7) to be assessed, and the appendix contains an honest failure case analysis (Appendix H) and limitations discussion (Appendix J).
The efficiency analysis in Table 6 makes a reasonable case that the native multi-turn paradigm reuses the KV cache and is faster than decoupled iterative baselines at higher accuracy on MLVU.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core recipe is assembled from existing components: DAPO for RL, over-turn masking directly from Mini-o3, a single VideoCrop tool analogous to VideoZoomer/Conan/Mini-o3, and a standard loss/attention-masking trick for multi-turn SFT. The paper's positioning as 'pioneering' native interleaved tool invocation overstates the delta relative to Mini-o3 and Conan, which are cited but not clearly differentiated experimentally.

The headline gains are small and fragile. Improvements over the strongest reproduced baselines are ~1.9 points on VideoMME (66.5 vs 64.6) and ~2.2 on MLVU (72.1 vs 69.9), within plausible evaluation variance; on MMR-V the SFT+RL variant (44.7) is actually worse than the RL-only variant (45.3), which the text does not acknowledge or explain.

The ablations provide only mixed support for the central technical claims. In Table 3, 'w/o gr. mask' matches or beats full TDAM on LVBench (44.1 vs 44.2) and LongVideoBench (57.1 vs 56.6), and the mask-ratio study (Table 11) shows the chosen 0.1 ratio yields at most ~1.8 average gain over no masking — weak evidence for a component promoted as a main contribution.

The multi-turn story is under-supported by the model's own behavior: Table 13 shows the average trajectory uses only 2.31 tool calls, and Table 5 shows most of the gain (63.6 to 66.5 on Video-MME) occurs between 2 and 8 turns. This suggests the framework's benefit may come mostly from one or two crops plus RL rather than the claimed deep multi-hop exploration.

The 'fake thinking' motivation for TDAM is anecdotal (two cases in Appendix I) and the fix — masking the global view during the answer phase for 10% of data — appears ad hoc, with no analysis of why this specific ratio is principled.

Potential train-test overlap is not addressed. A large fraction of the training data comes from LLaVA-Video and related corpora while evaluation uses MLVU, LongVideoBench, VideoMME, etc.; no decontamination audit or discussion is provided, which is essential to trust the SOTA claims.

The data pipeline depends on closed-source models (Gemini 2.5 Pro) for clue localization and trajectory generation, and 14.8k instances are self-collected YouTube videos; no release of code, data, or models is mentioned, and license/contamination details for the self-collected portion are thin, hurting reproducibility.

Baselines marked with '*' are the authors' own reproductions, and the reproduced LOVE-R1 and Video-Zoomer numbers differ from prior reports; the comparison protocol (16k initial visual quota) advantages Video-o3's design, and sensitivity of baselines to this quota is not analyzed.

Presentation has avoidable sloppiness that undermines confidence: malformed/duplicated grounding tags and a Chinese full-width comma inside JSON in the showcased examples (Figures 12-13), typos (e.g., 'demonstratedin'), and truncated prompt text in Figure 10 ('...is clear enoug').

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across eight video QA benchmarks plus temporal grounding (Charades-STA), with strong results (e.g., 72.1 MLVU, 46.5 Video-Holmes) and comparisons against the most relevant native multi-turn baselines (Conan, LongVT, VideoZoomer), several of which are re-run under a matched 16k visual-token quota for fairness.

Unusually thorough ablation suite: mask-ratio sweep (Table 11), reward-component ablations with training-dynamics curves (Figs. 8-9), turn-limit sweep (Table 5), turn-distribution analysis (Table 13), training-stage analysis (Table 14), and a scalability study with free-format data (Table 15). The Hybrid Clue Score's effect on grounding mIoU (Table 12) is a particularly convincing process-level validation.

Good reproducibility: full hyperparameter tables for SFT and RL, complete prompt templates, dataset composition with per-task source/instance counts (Table 8), and specification of evaluation tooling (VLMEvalKit, greedy decoding, 2 FPS sampling).

Honest limitations discussion (Appendix J) and explicit failure-case analysis (blind exploration exceeding turn limits, Fig. 14), plus a thoughtful impact statement addressing surveillance/privacy risks and data licensing.
Generalization check on a different, smaller base model (Qwen3-VL-4B, Table 7) and an efficiency comparison showing the shared-context KV-cache advantage over decoupled iterative methods (Table 6).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty relative to immediate prior work: the RL recipe (DAPO, over-turn masking, turn limits) is explicitly adopted from Mini-o3, and the overall 'think with videos'/iterative crop paradigm follows VideoZoomer, Conan, and LongVT. TDAM is a fairly simple visibility masking applied to only 10% of SFT data, and VTGR is heuristic reward shaping; neither is a deep methodological advance.

Several headline component ablations are within apparent noise, weakening the causal story. In Table 3, 'w/o gr. mask' scores 44.1/57.1/60.6/40.8 vs. full TDAM's 44.2/56.6/64.5/41.3, and 'w/o ans. mask' beats the baseline on three of four benchmarks; in Table 4, 'w/o Turn Decay Factor' beats full VTGR on LVBench (46.7 vs 47.5 is fine, but the deltas are mixed). No variance, seeds, or significance testing is reported for any SFT gains of +0.8-1.6.

Potential train-test contamination is not discussed: 418k of the Conventional training data comes from LLaVA-Video, whose source videos substantially overlap the videos underlying evaluation benchmarks such as VideoMME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench. The paper should report and quantify this overlap.

The claimed mechanism behind TDAM (masking the global overview during the answer phase to fix 'fake thinking') is trained-only; it is unclear whether the same visibility constraints are applied at inference, and Appendix I shows fake-thinking cases persist, suggesting the fix is partial. The 0.1 mask ratio also appears selected post hoc (Table 11), with only 51.6 vs 50.7 average separating it from alternatives.

The data pipeline depends on Gemini 2.5 Pro for clue localization, trajectory generation, and synthetic long-video data, which limits reproducibility for groups without access to that proprietary model and raises questions about how much of the performance comes from the proposed training techniques versus distillation from a much stronger teacher.

The comparison to decoupled/native prior work is strongest for reproduced baselines; several baselines in Table 1 are taken from original papers under potentially different visual budgets and frame settings, so the margins over some entries may be overstated.
